analysis.one_liner: Requires online services to get your opt-in consent before using, sharing, or selling your personal data.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it was introduced in April 2018 and died in the Senate Commerce Committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Federal Trade Commission to write rules requiring internet companies — search engines, social media platforms, streaming services — to tell you exactly what personal data they collect and how they use and share it. Companies would need your affirmative opt-in consent before using, sharing, or selling sensitive data like health information, location history, browsing history, and the content of your messages. It also required reasonable data security practices, breach notifications, rules against 'take-it-or-leave-it' privacy policies, and let state attorneys general sue to enforce it.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who uses a search engine, social network, streaming service, or app. Users would learn exactly what data is collected, would have to say yes before companies could use, share, or sell sensitive information like health records, precise location, browsing history, or the content of their messages, and would be notified of breaches. Companies could not refuse service to people who decline to consent, and state attorneys general could sue on residents' behalf.

how_it_helps.text: Edge providers — search engines, streaming services, social media — would have to notify customers about what sensitive data they collect, how they use and share it, and with whom [S2] [S3].

Companies would need opt-in consent before using, sharing, or selling sensitive personal information, including health, financial, precise location, browsing history, and content of communications [S2] [S3].

The bill would prohibit 'take-it-or-leave-it' offers, where a company refuses service unless the customer consents to data use, and would require disclosure of any discounts offered in exchange for consent [S3].

Edge providers would have to develop reasonable data security practices and notify customers after a security breach, and state attorneys general could bring civil actions to enforce the law and obtain restitution for residents [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Advertising-supported internet platforms and the broader adtech industry, whose business models depend on collecting, analyzing, and monetizing user data by default. They would face compliance costs and would lose the ability to use sensitive data without affirmative permission. Some smaller services might respond by charging subscription fees or offering fewer free, ad-supported features.

drawbacks.text: Opt-in consent is the strictest data-privacy standard; compliance costs would fall hardest on small firms and startups, and the largest platforms — which already have compliance teams — could be better positioned relative to smaller competitors [S3].

Many free online services are funded by advertising that depends on user data; stricter consent rules could lead companies to charge subscription fees, show fewer but less relevant ads, or restrict features, a cost honest supporters would acknowledge [S3].
The bill relies on the FTC to write and enforce detailed rules, so its real-world strength would depend on how the Commission defines key terms and how aggressively it enforces them [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — ordinary people deciding who gets their sensitive data — is substantial, since nearly every internet user is affected. The main costs are compliance burdens and possible changes to free, ad-supported services, which are real but modest compared with the privacy protections. The bill's weakness is procedural: much was left to future FTC rulemaking, so its final strength would have depended on the regulator, not the statute.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Markey, joined by Sen. Richard Blumenthal, introduced the CONSENT Act on April 10, 2018 [S1] [S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S5].
It drew three Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support [S4].
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies whose revenue depends on collecting, analyzing, and selling user data are better off: the opt-in consent and breach-notification rules they would have faced never arrived, and online privacy rules remain largely voluntary.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring FTC privacy rules and opt-in consent for online data collection.

against.name: John Thune
against.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Under his chairmanship the committee never held a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All four senators behind the bill were Democrats, and the record shows no Republican support and no committee action under the Republican-controlled Commerce Committee [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Online platforms (search, social media, streaming) and adtech
industries.note: These companies monetize user data, and opt-in consent for sensitive data plus a ban on take-it-or-leave-it terms would directly constrain that business model. The bill's death preserved the status quo in which users' data can be collected and sold under lengthy terms-of-service agreements.

industries.industry: Data brokers and data analytics firms
industries.note: The bill required strong protections on de-identified data and contractually barred re-identifying it, which would curb the market for buying, selling, and enriching consumer data. This market continues unchanged.
